title: How to Open a CDC Investor Account in Pakistan
summary: CDC investor accounts in Pakistan: what the account holds, sub-account vs Investor Account, documents needed, and what it does not cover.
body_markdown:
Before you can own a single share on the Pakistan Stock Exchange, the shares have to live somewhere. That somewhere is the Central Depository Company — CDC — which holds Pakistani listed securities in electronic form instead of paper certificates. Your broker executes the trade; CDC is the record of what you own afterwards. Most first-time investors in Pakistan never open a CDC account directly, because the sub-account their broker opens for them is already a CDC account. This guide covers what the account actually is, the two ways to hold one, what you need to open it, and what it does and does not protect.


## What a CDC account actually holds


A CDC account is a securities account, not a cash account. It records the shares, sukuk, Modaraba certificates and other listed instruments registered in your name. Your money sits with your broker or your bank; your securities sit in the depository.


That split matters more than it sounds. It means the question "where are my shares?" has an answer independent of your broker's own books. The depository record is the one that establishes ownership.


## The two ways to hold one


**A sub-account under your broker.** This is what almost everyone has. When you open a trading account with a brokerage, the brokerage — itself a CDC participant — opens a sub-account for you inside its own CDC participant account. You trade, and your holdings sit in that sub-account. It is the default because it is bundled into account opening and costs you nothing extra to arrange.


**An Investor Account directly with CDC.** Here you hold the account in your own name at the depository rather than inside a broker's structure. The appeal is separation: your securities are not held within a participant's account at all. The trade-off is that it is a second relationship to maintain, and you still need a broker to actually execute trades.


Which is right depends on how much you hold and how much you care about that separation. There is no universally correct answer, and anyone who tells you there is has not explained the trade-off.


## What you need to open an account


The documentary requirements are set by regulation rather than by individual brokers, so they are broadly consistent across the market:


- **A valid CNIC** (or NICOP/POC for overseas Pakistanis).
- **A bank account in your own name** , which is where dividends and sale proceeds are credited. Joint accounts and third-party accounts are not substitutes.
- **Proof of the bank relationship** — typically a cheque copy or a bank statement, so the mandate can be verified.
- **Tax status information** , because withholding on dividends differs between filers and non-filers.
- **Completed account-opening documentation** , which includes a risk disclosure you are expected to actually read.


Overseas Pakistanis have an additional route through the Roshan Digital Account framework, which was built to let non-resident Pakistanis invest without a local visit. If you are abroad, ask specifically about that rather than assuming the standard resident process applies.


## What the account does, and what it does not do


A CDC account establishes that you own particular securities. That is a narrow and valuable thing. It is not insurance, and it is worth being precise about what it does not cover.


It does not protect you from the price of those securities falling. It does not vet whether a company is a good business. It does not stop you from making a concentrated bet on one name. The depository is a record-keeper, and the record being accurate is orthogonal to the holdings being sensible.


It also does not consolidate your position for you. If you hold shares through two brokers, you have two sub-accounts and two sets of statements, and nothing in the depository stitches them into one view of what you own.


## Reading what you hold


CDC gives investors direct visibility into their own holdings, and brokers issue statements. Both are authoritative and neither is designed for the question most investors actually have, which is some version of "what is this worth today, and what has it done".


For that you need live prices applied to your holdings.[SuperX is a free PSX portfolio tracker](https://superx.pk/) that does exactly this — you can import a position list from a broker screenshot rather than typing it in, and it prices the portfolio against live market data, with real dividend history, Shariah status and zakat alongside. It is the fastest way we know of to turn a statement into a picture, and it costs nothing.


Whatever you use, the discipline is the same: reconcile what the tool shows against your CDC and broker statements periodically. The statements are the record of truth; a tracker is a lens on it. Once you can see the holdings, the next thing worth understanding is[what the KSE-100 actually measures](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/what-the-kse-100-actually-measures) , because that is the number your portfolio will be compared against.


## Common things that go wrong


**The bank mandate is stale.** Dividends are credited to the bank account on record. People change banks and forget to update the mandate, then wonder where a payout went.


**Tax status is out of date.** Filer status affects withholding on dividends. If your status changed and the record did not, the deduction will not match what you expected.


**Contact details are wrong.** Corporate actions, book-closure notices and AGM papers go to the address and email on record. A missed notice is a missed decision.


**Treating a sub-account as a savings product.** It is not. There is no return attached to the account itself.


## Where this fits if you are trying to earn


Opening the account is administrative. It is the step that makes investing possible, not the step that produces a return, and the gap between those two is where most people's expectations go wrong.

## Frequently asked questions


**Do I need a CDC account to buy shares in Pakistan?** You need your shares held in the depository, yes. In practice that happens through the sub-account your broker opens when you open a trading account, so you may already have one without having applied for it separately.


**Is a sub-account the same as a CDC Investor Account?** No. A sub-account sits inside your broker's participant account; an Investor Account is held in your own name directly at the depository. Both are CDC records of your holdings.


**Can I have accounts with more than one broker?** Yes, and many people do. Be aware that nothing consolidates the view for you — each relationship has its own statements.


**Where do my dividends go?** To the bank account recorded on your mandate, after applicable withholding. If the mandate is out of date, so is the destination.


**Can overseas Pakistanis open an account?** Yes — the Roshan Digital Account framework exists for precisely that. Ask your broker about that route specifically rather than the standard resident process.


**Does the depository guarantee my investment?** No. It records ownership accurately. It has nothing to say about whether what you own is worth holding.
